assumptions.summary: The focal organisms are summer annuals with a spring-to-autumn growth cycle and a winter seed bank.
Rainfall is instantaneous on the annual time scale and is the only soil-water input.
Soil-water evaporation is proportional to current water amount.
Flowering and fruiting occur in a regular short period represented by discrete events.
Root-system volume is proportional to average plant biomass.
Plants are spatially uniform, so average habitat area can proxy root overlap.
Plant counts remain fixed from germination to flowering and stress changes only average biomass.
Pairwise competition is linear in capacity-normalized biomass and derives from water use and root overlap.
Shrub hydraulic lift changes the herb uptake denominator in proportion to normalized shrub biomass.
Three regional annual rainfall values identify one lognormal distribution for the simulation.
A complete binary branching tree and half-sphere geometry represent desert root systems.
Mean annual total biomass and its unnormalized variance are adequate scale and stability criteria.
Poisson rain counts plus changed lognormal amounts adequately represent severe drought.
The reduced two-species within-year subsystem can be assessed independently of water, impulses, seeds, death, and facilitation.

contributions.summary: Use a seven-block Summary that mirrors model construction, each requested result, recommendations, and diagnostics.
Expose the progressive Growth-to-Competition-to-Facilitation route before the detailed mathematics.
Combine continuous biomass-water dynamics with rain, seed, germination, flowering, and death event maps.
Give directed competition coefficients an inspectable water-use and root-overlap interpretation.
Insert shrub hydraulic lift through one visible uptake-parameter interface.
Attempt to tie rainfall and root parameters to named literature values rather than leaving all coefficients arbitrary.
State the RK4 stages and event-ordered simulation procedure in a single pseudocode table.
Define explicit scale and fluctuation criteria before using a multi-objective richness ranking.
Compare facilitation, altered drought, pollution mechanisms, and habitat area through the same trajectory pipeline.
Translate distinct findings into preservation and modification action categories.
Sweep three literature-derived parameter families before the final quality claims.
Separate finite initial-condition recovery from a reduced analytical equilibrium discussion.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Annual precipitation depths 32.5, 113.2, and 360 mm are transferred from three distinct dryland regions and converted by the paper to 325, 1132, and 3600 kg over 10,000 square meters.
The three logged rainfall benchmarks [8.189, 7.032, 5.784]^T feed an unweighted normal-equation fit reported as mu=7.0017 and sigma=0.4008.
RS root length totals 3185.5 cm with 29.8 cm connections; NT totals 4802.5 cm with 49.0 cm connections.
Two taxon-specific root-volume factors are averaged into beta=108.9 and transferred to all simulated species.
Literature ranges c_i in [5,20], a_i in [10,50], and K_i below about 0.5 kg are used for species parameter choices without a calibration objective.
Table 2 names species traits, initial community state, horizon, beta-distributed rain timing, and lognormal rain amount as simulation inputs but supplies no executable configuration.
Figure 7 exposes ten annual mean values, ten variances, normalized columns, and ten benefit scores, but no TOPSIS weights or formulas.
The severe-drought scenario introduces a Poisson count variable tau and unspecified smaller mu and larger sigma.
Acid rain is encoded as c_i minus ten percent and smog as m_i plus ten percent without exposure data.
Habitat scenarios use 10,000, 15,000, and 20,000 square meters and report mean total biomasses about 476.9, 551.7, and 618.8 kg.
Sensitivity figures expose K_i values 0.45, 0.50, 0.55; theta_i values 1.8, 2.0, 2.2; and phi_i values 1.05, 1.20, 1.35 percent.
Initial biomass and plant count receive uniform disturbances whose support, dependence, seed, and replicate count are not stated.

K_i, theta_i, and phi_i sweeps rerun the core model one factor at a time.

Eq.36-Eq.37 analyze a reduced constant-coefficient slice of the competition model.

independent_extensions.summary: Calibrate a compound rainfall process with annual event count, event timing, event amount, serial dependence, seasonality, and conserved annual totals at one spatial scale.
Replace dimensional e^(1/R) facilitation with a dimensionless soil-water response that returns the competition baseline when no shrub is present and changes relative lift with drought.
Fit directed interaction coefficients from spatial root observations or field competition data, preserve index orientation, and clamp overlap through an explicit differentiable rule.
Control richness, composition, initial total abundance, habitat density, and trait distributions separately in biodiversity and shrub comparisons.
Publish the full TOPSIS matrix, criterion directions, normalization, weights, ideal points, distances, and weight-sensitivity crossings.
Use common random numbers and ensembles for drought, pollution, habitat, and initial-condition scenarios, reporting uncertainty and extinction or recovery metrics.
Run adaptive event-aware integration with positivity controls and compare step refinements against a trusted solver on the same impulse schedule.
Analyze the full periodic hybrid system or a justified averaged model, including water, seed bank, event maps, and dynamic competition, instead of calling coexistence positivity full stability.
Turn viability actions into intervention variables with costs, feasibility, ecological side effects, larger-environment metrics, and uncertainty-aware decision tradeoffs.

models.section: 4.1 Eq.8-Eq.12 seed-bank and annual phenology event maps
models.summary: Eq.8 updates the seed bank; Eq.9 collects continuous growth; Eq.10 repeats the rain jump; Eq.11 converts biomass to seeds; Eq.12 resets plants and germinates the next generation.
Eq.13 adds sigma_21 and sigma_12; Eq.14 normalizes relative water-use capacities; Eq.15 maps overlap and capacity ratios to directed competition coefficients.

models.section: 4.2 Eq.16-Eq.18 root geometry and average overlap
models.summary: Eq.16 assumes a half-sphere and V_i=beta_i B_i; Eq.17 derives projected coverage; Eq.18 subtracts equal per-plant habitat share from coverage to estimate overlap.
Eq.19 couples two biomass states to R; Eq.20 repeats the sigma, overlap, and water-use normalization rules.
Eq.21 restores c_i f_i(R)-m_i in each biomass derivative and sums all competitors and water use; Eq.22 defines every directed coefficient, overlap proxy, and normalized water-use weight.
Eq.23 introduces shrub biomass and an indicator delta_j; Eq.24 multiplies the modified denominator by e^(1/R) to represent drought dependence.
Eq.25 maps the three reported annual masses to mu and sigma through log-scale center and plus/minus-three-sigma equations; Eq.26 solves the overdetermined system by normal equations.

models.section: 4.4 Eq.27-Eq.30 binary-root geometry and universal scale factor
models.summary: Eq.27 assumes a complete equal-edge binary tree; Eq.28 infers z about seven; Eq.29 converts branch depth and edge length to a radial diameter; Eq.30 averages two taxon-specific beta values.
Eq.31 evaluates four slopes at the start, two midpoints, and endpoint and combines them with 1:2:2:1 weights; Table 2 adds yearly germination, rainfall jumps, flowering conversion, and death events.
Eq.32 sums average biomass times abundance; Eq.33 averages yearly totals; Eq.34 computes population variance over k_max years.
Eq.35 reports variance (0.1 times the initial value)^2/12 for either biomass or abundance disturbance.
Eq.36 lists four equilibria; Eq.37 substitutes root-overlap expressions and states sigma_12<1 and sigma_21<1 as desired coexistence requirements.
The paper names TOPSIS and prints normalized Average, Variance, and Benefit Evaluation columns but omits the normalization, cost conversion, weights, ideal points, distances, and closeness equation.

results_trace.summary: short-and-long horizon pairing: one-year event phases -> 30-year maxima -> hybrid behavior preview. Boundary: A paired visual should state which statistic is plotted at each horizon.

multi-species trajectory demonstration: one-year rain/flower/death -> 30-year species separation -> competition behavior. Boundary: A single run demonstrates mechanics but not expected stochastic performance.
dual-objective framing: higher total weight + lower extreme fluctuation -> scale/stability balance. Boundary: Indicator choice should reflect stakeholder utility and ecological meaning.
metric construction: species mean biomass*n_i -> yearly M -> horizon mean E -> variance var. Boundary: Retain units, horizon, denominator, and whether yearly peaks or endpoints are used.
decision-matrix ranking: type number 1-10 -> normalized average/variance -> benefit evaluation. Boundary: Ranking requires visible criterion weights and ideal-point computation.

richness-tradeoff finding: increase species input -> lower total weight -> lower fluctuation. Boundary: Hold composition, total individuals, and parameter distributions comparable when interpreting count effects.

competition-based explanation: more competition -> limited extreme growth -> balanced proportions -> stability. Boundary: This is a model-based explanation and should not be presented as external causal confirmation.

minimum-richness decision: TOPSIS index above one-species row -> more than/eight species -> overall benefit. Boundary: Resolve the source's at-least-eight versus more-than-eight wording and strict inequality.

coefficient-heterogeneity premise: larger c_i differences -> greater total biomass -> lower stability. Boundary: A coefficient-dispersion claim needs controlled sweeps and an explicit stability metric.
shrub-ablation design: three herbages + shrub -> competition+cooperation; three herbages -> competition only. Boundary: The comparison also changes richness and initial composition unless controlled.

shrub scale-stability finding: shrub community dotted line -> lower E + much smaller var -> scale/stability tradeoff. Boundary: Report exact values and uncertainty rather than line-style interpretation alone.
facilitation-to-diversity interpretation: shrub water lift -> reduced herb competition -> biodiversity maintenance. Boundary: A biomass plot does not directly measure biodiversity persistence.

rainfall-regime visualization: severe count/amount process -> sparse low rainfall; comparison -> less-frequent pattern. Boundary: Axes, parameters, realization seed, and scenario labels must be explicit.

severe-drought trajectory finding: normal versus severe drought -> total/individual biomass -> lower scale and stability. Boundary: Separate average level, variance, extinction frequency, and stochastic uncertainty.

drought-richness ledger: types 4/6/8/10/12/24 -> average decreases -> variance decreases. Boundary: A declining variance with declining mean may require normalization before it is called higher stability.

two-path pollutant encoding: smog raises m_i -> scale effect; acid rain lowers c_i -> scale + stability effect. Boundary: Matched 10% parameter changes are not necessarily matched environmental severities.

pollutant panel comparison: normal vs acid-rain/smog trajectories -> E/Var summaries -> hazard interpretation. Boundary: Use exact panel-to-caption mapping and state whether E/Var values share the same random forcing.

stressor-specific stability contrast: both lower scale -> acid rain lowers stability more -> water-use interpretation. Boundary: The mechanism interpretation should distinguish what is encoded from what is observed.
area-biomass response finding: smaller area -> lower mean biomass -> more inferred root intersections. Boundary: The spatial explanation must be implemented, not only narrated after the plot.

preservation action synthesis: intrinsic robustness -> preserve naturalness -> biodiversity/water/pollution/habitat actions. Boundary: Preservation claims should link each action to a result and an accountable actor.

modification action synthesis: remaining vulnerability -> introduce suitable species + irrigation facilities. Boundary: Interventions need compatibility, resource, cost, and unintended-effect analysis.

cross-parameter trajectory finding: K_i/theta_i/phi_i variants -> multi-species trajectories -> diminishing long-term differences. Boundary: Visual convergence needs a quantified response metric and random-replicate control.
initial-condition recovery finding: random initial perturbations -> long-run maximum biomass curves -> stability claim. Boundary: One plotted realization cannot establish stochastic stability.

coexistence-condition finding: four equilibria -> coexistence point P3 -> sigma_12<1 and sigma_21<1 -> reasonableness. Boundary: Local coexistence conditions also require positivity, Jacobian eigenvalues, and the shared-water state.

task_reconstruction.decision: Use the paper as a traceable hybrid-model and scenario-writing example, but treat numerical thresholds and recommendations as conditional because rainfall units, parameter transfer, TOPSIS settings, stochastic design, solver controls, and empirical validation are incomplete or inconsistent.

task_reconstruction.objective: For dryland ecologists and plant-community managers, model annual-plant biomass under irregular rainfall, competition, and shrub facilitation; determine a conditional richness benefit; test composition, drought, pollution, and habitat changes; and recommend long-term viability actions.
outputs: single- and multi-species biomass, soil-water, and seed-bank trajectories
root-derived directed competition and shrub-facilitation parameters

weaknesses.summary: Eq.3 tends to 1/d_i as R grows, while Table 1 calls d_i the upper limit, reversing the stated parameter role.
Eq.4 defines one rain-event timing density but supplies no annual event-count distribution in the baseline model.
Eq.6 omits plant count n_i even though Eq.19 and Eq.21 later multiply per-plant uptake by abundance.
Eq.12 initializes next-year biomass from the seed bank without visibly depleting the germinated seed stock.
Eq.13, Eq.21, and Eq.22 do not keep the sigma_ij versus sigma_ji direction consistent.
Eq.14 states only lambda_1+lambda_2=1 and omits the mapping from water-use capacities to the normalized weights.
Eq.15 and the later overlap equations do not implement the prose-required zero clamp when estimated overlap is negative.
Eq.19 uses c_i R-m_i while Eq.13 and Eq.21 use c_i f_i(R)-m_i, changing the growth mechanism without explanation.
Eq.24 contains e^(1/R) although R is listed in kg; the exponent is dimensional, the no-shrub case does not return Eq.23's baseline, and the relative shrub effect is independent of R.
The claimed 95 percent interval uses plus/minus three sigma; a normal three-sigma interval is about 99.73 percent.
Over 10,000 square meters, 32.5 mm water has mass 325,000 kg, not 325 kg; all three reported masses are low by a factor of 1000.
Annual precipitation totals are used to calibrate Eq.5's per-event rainfall amount without a count or allocation model.
For lognormal rainfall E[exp(zeta)]=exp(mu+sigma^2/2), not exp(mu), so the stated mean mapping is wrong.
Eq.27-Eq.30 assume complete equal-edge binary trees, straight radial roots, half-sphere volume, and a universal beta from two taxa without uncertainty.
RK4 accuracy is conditional on step size and smoothness, yet no step, event localization, convergence, stiffness, or positivity control is reported.
The TOPSIS normalization, cost-direction conversion, weights, ideal points, distances, and closeness formula are omitted.
Figure 7 first crosses the one-species score at eight species, while page 17 says more than eight and the Summary says at least eight.
The shrub comparison uses four species versus three, confounding shrub facilitation with richness, composition, and initial-total differences.
The severe-drought scenario changes event count, amount center, and amount spread together and reports no ensemble or matched randomness.
Lower variance under lower biomass is labeled greater stability without normalization, recovery, persistence, or extinction metrics.
Acid rain and smog are each represented by an arbitrary ten-percent parameter change without exposure-response calibration or matched severity.
Habitat reduction changes an area term inside average overlap but does not simulate locations, density redistribution, boundaries, or recruitment.
Recommendations on irrigation, introductions, pollution, and habitat lack feasibility, cost, ecological compatibility, and larger-environment outcomes.
Eq.35 leaves the uniform support unstated; the displayed variance corresponds to plus/minus five percent when 0.1 times the state is the total width, not plus/minus ten percent.
Figure 16 shows three trajectories under initial perturbations but no distributional recovery metric, replicate count, or stochastic stability proof.
Eq.36-Eq.37 freeze water and dynamic sigma, omit impulses, seeds, death, and facilitation, and give positivity rather than Jacobian stability conditions.
The strength claim that RK4 provides strong stability is unsupported without solver-refinement or error analysis.
No code, parameter file, random seed, simulation output, or environment is attached, so Eq.1-Eq.37 and Figures 3-16 are not end-to-end reproducible.
